title: Neurobiology of EMDR
subtitle: Established clinical efficacy with unsettled mechanisms
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating neurobiology of emdr across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
tags: established efficacy for PTSD; mechanisms mixed
searchTerms: established efficacy for PTSD; mechanisms mixed
learningObjectives: Explain neurobiology of emdr in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in neurobiology of emdr.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to neurobiology of emdr.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR is a structured psychotherapy that uses trauma recall with bilateral stimulation within a broader eight-phase protocol.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Clinical efficacy for PTSD is supported by guidelines, while proposed mechanisms include working-memory taxation, orienting responses, extinction and memory updating.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Neuroimaging studies report changes after treatment, but small samples and non-specific therapy effects limit causal conclusions.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of neurobiology of emdr as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need neurobiology of emdr to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not present one neural mechanism as proven.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use neurobiology of emdr to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses neurobiology of emdr to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not present one neural mechanism as proven. Evidence classification: established efficacy for PTSD; mechanisms mixed.
